name: Fermi level
seoTitle: Fermi level Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Fermi level: work out fermi energy from the energy and the temperature. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the energy and the temperature and the Fermi level calculator solves for fermi energy. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Fermi level calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fermi level calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports fermi energy in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the material); then you type in the energy and the temperature.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 18 options, such as cu (copper), ag (silver) and au (gold). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in electronvolts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 33 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kelvins. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fermi level calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fermi wave number=1000000000 × (30) × (PI ^ 2 ÷ 3) × (number density of electrons)
Fermi wave number=(45546917800 ÷ 5272859) × fermi velocity
Fermi wave number=(1140000000 ÷ 5272859) × the square root of (561512830485370) × the square root of (fermi energy)
Fermi temperature=(400544158500 ÷ 34516213) × fermi energy
Function intermediate=((500 ÷ 34516213) × (-801088317 × fermi energy + 5000000000000000000000000000 × energy) ÷ temperature)
Fermi function=(25000, ((500 ÷ 34516213) × (-801088317 × fermi energy + 5000000000000000000000000000 × energy) ÷ temperature)) ÷ ((25000, ((500 ÷ 34516213) × (-801088317 × fermi energy + 5000000000000000000000000000 × energy) ÷ temperature)) + (67957, ((500 ÷ 34516213) × (-801088317 × fermi energy + 5000000000000000000000000000 × energy) ÷ temperature)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Energy, opening in electronvolts
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Energy, opening in electronvolts
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fermi level calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the energy and the temperature — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fermi level calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns fermi energy, derived from the energy and the temperature. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fermi level calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the energy and the temperature, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter number density of electrons in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Number density of electrons opens in cubic meters and the chip beside it offers 40 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number density of electrons = 0 m³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fermi level calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
